analysis.one_liner: Bars states from taxing out-of-state businesses unless they have a physical presence there.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill and leaders prepared it for floor debate, but no vote was ever held in either chamber before the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten federal rules, dating to 1959, that limit when states can tax businesses based outside their borders. It would have barred states from imposing income taxes and a long list of other business taxes on any out-of-state company unless that company had employees, property, or agents in the state for more than 21 days a year. Today only sales of physical goods are protected; the bill would have extended that shield to services, software, and intangible property, and to gross-receipts, franchise, and similar state business taxes [S2] [S3] [S4]. The practical effect: a company could sell to customers in a state, or send people there for up to 21 days a year, without owing that state any business taxes.
analysis.who_benefits: Multistate corporations — national service firms, software and intangible-property sellers, and large remote sellers of goods — would owe less in state income, gross-receipts, and franchise taxes, because most of their activity in a state would no longer create a taxable 'physical presence' [S2] [S3] [S4].

how_it_helps.text: Extends the federal prohibition on state net income taxation from sales of tangible goods to all forms of property, including intangible property and services [S2] [S3] [S4].

Blocks states from imposing income taxes and other business activity taxes — including gross-receipts, franchise, business-license, and capital-stock taxes — on out-of-state businesses without a physical presence in the taxing state [S3] [S4].

Defines physical presence as more than 21 days a year of business activity in the state, and excludes activities such as purchasing, news gathering, meeting officials, attending conferences, and charity work from that count [S3] [S4].

Preserves limited state taxing power with one-day triggers for local sales completed in-state, services affecting real property, and live performances and sporting events before audiences of more than 100 [S3] [S4].

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments would lose revenue they currently collect from out-of-state companies, forcing higher taxes on residents and in-state businesses or cuts to state-funded services. In-state businesses, which still owe their own state's taxes, would compete against exempt out-of-state rivals. The bill explicitly excludes sales, use, and similar taxes from its prohibition, so consumers' sales taxes on purchases would be untouched [S3] [S4].

drawbacks.text: States would lose business tax revenue from out-of-state companies, shifting the burden onto residents and locally based firms or forcing cuts to state services — the bill restricts a broad set of state business taxes, not just income taxes [S3] [S4].

The 21-day physical presence threshold would allow a company to do substantial business in a state — sending employees, agents, and leased property there for weeks — without owing it business taxes, putting in-state businesses that do pay at a competitive disadvantage [S3] [S4].

Supporters' counterargument: the bill creates one predictable national rule for multistate companies, ending inconsistent state tax assertions and the compliance costs and legal disputes that come with them [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For large multistate companies, the bill offered real savings and simpler compliance. For the public, the trade was poor: state revenue that funds schools, roads, and services would shrink, and the cost would land on state residents and in-state businesses, while the bill exempted sales and use taxes paid directly by consumers — meaning the shield was built for business taxes, not consumer ones.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee approved it by voice vote, it was placed on the Union Calendar, and a House Rules Committee resolution was reported to govern floor debate — but the House never voted on it and the Senate never acted before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced April 28, 2005 by Rep. Goodlatte with original cosponsors from both parties, and referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S1] [S5] [S6].
The Judiciary Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law held hearings and forwarded it to the full committee by voice vote in December 2005 [S6].
The full Judiciary Committee approved an amended version by voice vote in June 2006 and reported it to the House with House Report 109-575 on July 17, 2006 [S6] [S4].

It was placed on the Union Calendar, and on July 24, 2006 a Rules Committee resolution (H. Res. 939) was reported providing for one hour of debate with the bill closed to amendments — the usual setup for a floor vote [S6].
No House floor vote followed, and the bill received no action in the Senate; the 109th Congress ended January 3, 2007 [S1] [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and local governments kept the authority to tax out-of-state businesses, and in-state businesses avoided a new disadvantage against exempt out-of-state competitors. Multistate corporations, which stood to save on state business taxes, lost the opportunity.

for.name: Rep. Bob Goodlatte
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and guided it through the House Judiciary Committee, which reported it amended [S1] [S4] [S6].

for.name: 40 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including additional sponsors added when it was reported in July 2006 [S4] [S5].

for.name: Business Activity Tax Coalition
for.what_they_did: Longstanding coalition of multistate companies that pushed for federal limits on state business taxation of this kind.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor schedule
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote, despite the Rules Committee reporting a rule for its consideration in July 2006 [S6].

against.name: United States Senate (109th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; it was never referred to committee or considered [S1] [S6].

against.name: National Governors Association and Multistate Tax Commission
against.what_they_did: Opposed congressional limits on state taxing authority of this kind, which would cut state revenue.

sides.party_line_note: No recorded votes exist — every committee action was by voice vote — but sponsorship leaned heavily Republican: 35 of 40 cosponsors were Republicans, with 5 Democrats [S5].

industries.industry: Multistate corporations and national service and software sellers
industries.note: The bill would have exempted them from state income, gross-receipts, franchise, and similar taxes unless they had more than 21 days of physical presence in a state [S3] [S4]. The revenue they avoided would come from state budgets, which are paid for by residents and local businesses.

States would lose the ability to tax most out-of-state business activity, reducing revenue that funds services residents rely on. The bill explicitly carved out sales and use taxes, leaving that consumer revenue intact [S3] [S4].

They would keep owing their own state's business taxes while out-of-state competitors selling into the same market were exempt — a competitive disadvantage. Their interest ran with the public's, since both benefit from out-of-state firms paying into state budgets.

Retailers shipping goods into a state without a physical presence already enjoyed protection under the 1959 federal law; the bill preserved that. The bill deliberately did not touch states' sales and use taxes, so their customers' taxes were unchanged [S2] [S4].
